title: Passive therapies: what to know
intro: Passive therapies are treatments that are done to you rather than requiring your own active effort, such as massage, heat or cold packs, ultrasound, electrotherapy and manual therapy. Many people find them soothing, but they usually work best as a supplement to active measures like exercise, not as the sole treatment.

sections.heading: What counts as passive
paragraphs: Examples include massage, hot packs, fango, hot baths, cold packs, ultrasound, electrical nerve stimulation, traction, mobilisation and manipulation by a therapist, and lymphatic drainage. They are used for back and neck pain, joint problems, muscle tension and recovery after injury.

sections.heading: What they can do
paragraphs: Heat can relax muscles and relieve stiffness for a short time. Cold can reduce swelling and numb pain after acute injury. Massage and manual therapy may offer short-term relief of pain and tension. Many people value the sense of care and relaxation, which can also help with pain coping.

sections.heading: What evidence shows
paragraphs: For many conditions, the benefits of passive treatments are modest and short-lived. Studies suggest that for conditions like back pain and osteoarthritis, exercise and education provide longer-lasting improvement. Some treatments, such as ultrasound or traction, show little proven benefit. Evidence varies by treatment and condition.

sections.heading: Risks and costs
paragraphs: Most passive therapies are safe when done properly. Heat can burn skin, especially with reduced sensation. Spinal manipulation carries a small risk of complications and is not suitable for everyone. Health insurance may cover only some treatments, and you may pay for others, so it is worth asking about costs and expected benefit.

sections.heading: Using them wisely
paragraphs: Combine passive treatments with active therapy, such as exercise, where this is advised. Ask a therapist to set goals and review progress after a limited number of sessions. If pain relief is only brief and function does not improve, discuss alternatives. Be wary of promises of cures or long courses of treatment with no review.

examples.title: Setting goals
examples.text: Imagine you have back pain and receive weekly massage. You could ask your therapist to also teach you exercises that you can do at home, and agree how to judge progress.

examples.title: Using heat safely
examples.text: Suppose you use a hot pack for neck tension. You might place a cloth between pack and skin, limit it to about twenty minutes and stop if the skin turns red.
